targets: pipelines for R that only rebuild what changed

The problem it solves

An analysis starts as one long R script. Soon it takes ten minutes to run, and every small change means running everything from the top, or, worse, running only the lines you remember and trusting that the rest is still up to date. A month later you are not sure that the figure in the paper comes from the current data.

The general idea

targets turns the script into a pipeline. Each step, a target, is a named R object computed by a function. targets stores the results, remembers which code and which upstream objects each one depends on, and on the next run rebuilds only what is outdated. The dependency graph comes from the code itself, so there is nothing to wire up by hand.

Examples

# _targets.R
library(targets)
library(tarchetypes)
tar_option_set(packages = c("dplyr", "readr"))

list(
  tar_target(raw,   read_csv("data/raw.csv")),
  tar_target(clean, raw |> filter(!is.na(price))),
  tar_target(model, lm(price ~ rooms, data = clean)),
  tar_quarto(report, "report.qmd")
)
tar_make()          # build what is outdated
tar_visnetwork()    # draw the dependency graph
tar_read(model)     # load a result

Tips from my setup

  • Functions in R/, a thin _targets.R. The pipeline file only lists the steps, and the logic lives in functions in an R/ folder, which keeps both readable and testable.
  • Feed a Quarto document. I tried it on a project where the pipeline's results flow into a Quarto manuscript, so the numbers and figures in the text always come from the current run. See the post about Quarto.
  • Why I moved on. targets is wonderful if everything is R. My work became Python first, and I wanted one tool for data, parameters and experiments, so the pipelines moved to Snakemake and then to DVC. The idea, though, is the same, and it is the one I took with me: a pipeline is a graph of steps that knows what is outdated.
